entries.note: The sweeping characterization of enthusiasts as victims or con artists is polemical.

entries.test: Multiply the stated 190GW by Huang's stated $80–100 billion per GW and compare the result with $9.5–15 trillion.
entries.note: The stated inputs imply $15.2–19 trillion; the conditional arithmetic is already testable.

entries.test: Public construction financing and annual bank debt issuance would show whether completing the planned capacity requires $500 billion–$1 trillion of bank debt annually.
entries.note: The current $250 billion figure is explicitly his estimate.

entries.test: NVIDIA customer concentration disclosures, customers' financing records, and purchasing capacity over time would test the claimed dependence and shrinking buyer pool.
entries.note: The normalization drops the material qualifier that firms must afford thousands of $7.8 million racks.

entries.test: Hyperscaler equity issuance records and contemporaneous borrowing terms, credit availability, and financing disclosures would test whether debt was becoming harder to obtain.
entries.note: He adopts the interpretation while crediting Kedrosky.

entries.test: Anthropic's revenue, available financing, and compute payment obligations through 2029 would show whether $174 billion in annual revenue is necessary to pay its commitments.
Anthropic's financing, cash flow, and expenditures through June 8, 2027 would establish whether it needed at least $200 billion beyond the cited $95 billion.
entries.note: Raising money alone would not establish that the full amount was necessary.

entries.test: OpenAI's financing, cash flow, and payment obligations through December 2026 would establish whether it required at least $250 billion beyond its March round.
Industry revenue and infrastructure operating, financing, and contractual costs through 2030 would test whether annual revenue above $2 trillion is necessary for financial viability.
entries.note: The surrounding text gives 'make sense' a financial viability reading.

entries.test: If annual industry revenue remains below the stated threshold in 2030, public financial records would show whether the buildout is viable and Anthropic and OpenAI can pay their commitments.

entries.note: 'I wouldn’t be surprised' explicitly expresses a possibility.

entries.test: Public estimates of total AI compute spending and the spending attributable to Anthropic and OpenAI would test the asserted minimum 70% share.
entries.note: The 70% floor is firm; the higher range is tentative.

entries.test: Public AI compute purchasing estimates excluding Anthropic and OpenAI, alongside those firms' annual losses, would test the stated amounts.
Operating costs, debt service, and revenues for half the planned capacity would establish whether about $875 billion annually is required to avoid cash shortfalls.
Anthropic's publicly reported financial results through 2029 would show whether it becomes profitable.
entries.note: In context, 'I do not believe it will be' expresses his negative forecast.

entries.test: Anthropic's financial results at publication, with accounting adjustments and financing effects separated from operating performance, would show whether it was profitable.
entries.note: The exception does not assert that financial engineering actually makes it profitable.

entries.test: Public compute contracts and spending disclosures would identify any comparably large purchasers outside the named companies and hyperscalers.
entries.note: The following discussion supplies scale and mentions Jane Street as an exception.

entries.test: Each company's monthly revenue by Q1 2028, financing, and compute obligations would test whether revenue below $10 billion monthly can support its commitments.
Annual revenue growth and ability to fund commitments through 2029–2030 would test whether both companies must approximately double each year.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion identifies business size primarily with revenue.

entries.test: If OpenAI stops purchasing its contracted compute because of inability or unwillingness to pay, Oracle's cash flow and liquidity disclosures would show whether it runs out of money.
Following credit concerns about Oracle or OpenAI, disclosed collateral values and loan maintenance requirements would show whether Ellison faces large margin-call exposure.
entries.note: He predicts a threat of margin calls, not necessarily their execution.

entries.test: Anthropic's annual revenue, available funds, and contractual payments by June 2028 would show whether exceeding $100 billion in revenue is necessary to afford its commitments.
Aggregate AI company compute spending at publication and in 2030, together with data center costs and revenues, would test the current ceiling and claimed trillion-dollar viability requirement.
entries.note: The present spending component is already testable.

entries.test: Company revenues and compute purchases through 2030 would test whether each firm needs about $400 billion annually to support the asserted compute demand.
entries.note: The source says both companies need that revenue; the normalization leaves unclear whether $400 billion is each or combined.

entries.test: Microsoft's AI revenue breakdown would show whether OpenAI compute supplies most of the $37 billion run rate and how much comes from Copilot.
entries.note: The normalization adds 'similar products' and strengthens the tentative $8 billion estimate. The majority-share assertion is firm.
'AI stories' has no shared threshold for business activity, strategy, or success.

entries.test: Buildout costs and financing requirements would show whether $500 billion of annual purchases still leaves at least $250 billion in required compute revenue.
entries.note: The hypothetical spending scenario is a prospective condition.

entries.test: Public task-level studies documenting AI costs and attributable financial benefits would establish whether task cost and ROI can be measured.
entries.note: A documented successful measurement can falsify the categorical impossibility claim.

entries.test: AI revenue growth data around the reported enterprise spending caps would show whether growth was slowing.

entries.note: 'Likely' qualifies the predicted further slowdown.

entries.test: Longitudinal enterprise spending, renewal, and retention records would show whether revenues persist when customers lack visibility into costs.
entries.note: The claim concerns the future durability of this revenue stream.

entries.test: Contemporaneous AI revenue and enterprise spending growth data would show whether commercial growth was slowing.
entries.note: The surrounding section supplies a commercial growth reading of 'AI is slowing down.'

entries.test: Representative evidence on adoption, utility, and security vulnerabilities in LLM-created applications would test whether the vast majority are useless and insecure.
entries.note: The insulting wording accompanies substantive claims about application outcomes.

entries.test: Aggregate publicly documented AI industry expenditures through publication would test whether spending exceeded $1 trillion.
entries.note: In context, 'burned' refers to money spent on AI, not specifically accounting net losses.

entries.test: Published pricing and subscription changes by both companies would show whether they raise customer charges.
entries.note: IPO pursuit is asserted as ongoing, not a hypothetical antecedent. The normalization makes subscription cuts firm despite their placement within the 'very likely' passage.

entries.test: Subsequent technology coverage would show whether agent loops become a prominent new subject of enthusiastic reporting.
entries.note: 'I expect' is a firm expectation under the stated rules.

entries.test: Public generative AI operating costs, revenues, and sustained profitability would test the categorical claim of economic unviability.
entries.note: The economic assertion supplies a testable core despite evaluative adjectives.

entries.test: Public provider financials and documented task-level cost and ROI measurements would test the claimed lack of viable economics and measurable returns.
Historical provider costs and customer prices for comparable AI services would show whether costs have ever fallen.
entries.note: The categorical 'only ever increased' assertion is testable.
The claim attributes a private motive. The normalization also converts wanting high costs into deliberately keeping costs high.

entries.test: Following a publicly documented profitability drive, compute purchases and resulting cloud and NVIDIA demand would test the predicted reductions.
entries.note: The normalization drops sustainability as an alternative trigger and the explicit assumption that profitability or sustainability is possible.

entries.test: Public customer deployment records and per-user service costs versus payments would test whether revenues come from experiments or subsidies worth hundreds of dollars per user.
entries.note: The subsidy amount provides a concrete factual component.

entries.test: Repeated enterprise surveys and public purchasing decisions would show whether skepticism about AI spending increases after publication.
entries.note: The context identifies 'worse' with increasing doubts about value.

entries.test: Public technical disclosures and financial results could establish whether a breakthrough already held at publication delivers substantial ROI or lowers total costs without reducing compute spending.
entries.note: An undisclosed technical capability can later be publicly documented; secrecy alone does not make it inherently uncheckable.

entries.test: The companies' required revenue trajectories, profitability, and financing under their commitments, compared with historical corporate growth records, would test the claimed requirements.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion places the next few years within the 2029–2030 buildout horizon.

entries.test: Buildout costs, contracted purchases, and additional customer demand would show whether at least $250 billion in further annual compute revenue is required.
entries.note: The dollar requirement is firm; needing two additional companies is explicitly tentative.

entries.test: Public employee surveys, testimony, and comparisons before and after AI mandates would test whether those mandates increased opposition to leadership.
entries.note: Workforce attitudes and their causes can be investigated through public empirical evidence.
'Possibly' qualifies bursting the bubble. The two-week horizon concerns publication, not the bubble's collapse.
